 library(ggpubr)
drug_consumption <- fetch_ucirepo(id=373)

cat(drug_consumption$"metadata"$additional_info$summary)
Database contains records for 1885 respondents. For each respondent 12 attributes are known: Personality measurements which include NEO-FFI-R (neuroticism, extraversion, openness to experience, agreeableness, and conscientiousness), BIS-11 (impulsivity), and ImpSS (sensation seeking), level of education, age, gender, country of residence and ethnicity. All input attributes are originally categorical and are quantified. After quantification values of all input features can be considered as real-valued. In addition, participants were questioned concerning their use of 18 legal and illegal drugs (alcohol, amphetamines, amyl nitrite, benzodiazepine, cannabis, chocolate, cocaine, caffeine, crack, ecstasy, heroin, ketamine, legal highs, LSD, methadone, mushrooms, nicotine and volatile substance abuse and one fictitious drug (Semeron) which was introduced to identify over-claimers. For each drug they have to select one of the answers: never used the drug, used it over a decade ago, or in the last decade, year, month, week, or day.
Database contains 18 classification problems. Each of independent label variables contains seven classes: "Never Used", "Used over a Decade Ago", "Used in Last Decade", "Used in Last Year", "Used in Last Month", "Used in Last Week", and "Used in Last Day".

Problem which can be solved:
* Seven class classifications for each drug separately.
* Problem can be transformed to binary classification by union of part of classes into one new class. For example, "Never Used", "Used over a Decade Ago" form class "Non-user" and all other classes form class "User".
* The best binarization of classes for each attribute.
* Evaluation of risk to be drug consumer for each drug.

Detailed description of database and process of data quantification are presented in E. Fehrman, A. K. Muhammad, E. M. Mirkes, V. Egan and A. N. Gorban, "The Five Factor Model of personality and evaluation of drug consumption risk.," arXiv https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.06297, 2015
Paper above solve binary classification problem for all drugs. For most of drugs sensitivity and specificity are greater than 75%.
  1. In one paragraph (between 150 and 250 words) describe the dataset you have chosen. Specifically, you need to describe the relationships between the numerical and categorical variables you have chosen.

The dataset we chose for this project contains both numeric and categorical variables for 1885 respondents. The numerical variables we analyzed include the NEO-FFI-FR personality measurements: nscore (Neuroticism score), escore (Extraversion score), and oscore (Openness to Experience score). The categorical variables that we examined include alcohol, cannabis and nicotine (usage levels), which are broken down into different consumption categories. The categories range from CL0, meaning the respondent has never used the drug, to CL6, which means they have used the drug in the last day when surveyed. Our analysis explores how these personality traits relate to consumption levels for each drug. For example, individuals with higher neuroticism scores may have increased consumption due to behaviors related with stress, while those with higher extraversion scores might be linked to more frequent alcohol and nicotine consumption in social settings. In addition, individuals with higher openness to experience scores may be more open to experimentation with substances. Analyzing this dataset can help uncover behavioral risk patterns and provide insights into how personality traits correlate with drug consumption. Lastly, another analysis we can make is the population of each substance consumed, precisely how many people have used alcohol, cannabis, and or nicotine, and compare the frequencies.

df_drugs <- drug_consumption$data$original

drugs_summary <- df_drugs |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(nscore, escore, oscore), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") |>
  summarize(
    min = round(min(value), 8),
    mean = round(mean(value), 8),
    median = round(median(value), 8),
    max = round(max(value), 8),
    sd = round(sd(value), 8),
    .by = "variable"
  )

For the nscore variable, the median is higher than the mean, indicating that the data is left skewed, meaning there is a tail on the left side. However, for the oscore variable, the mean is higher than the median. This indicates that the data is right skewed, meaning that there is a tail on the right side.

In analyzing the survey data on alcohol, nicotine, and cannabis use, we observed distinct patterns in the consumption habits of respondents. For alcohol, 34 individuals reported no consumption, 1,341 participants fell into the moderate consumption categories (CL1-CL5), and 505 were categorized as very heavy drinkers (CL6). This indicates that 1.8% of respondents abstained from alcohol, while 26.79% identified as very heavy drinkers. In contrast, cannabis use showed that 413 respondents reported no use, 1,009 fell into the moderate consumption categories, and 463 stated they used it daily (CL6). This means that 21.9% of respondents did not use cannabis, while 24.56% were classified as heavy cannabis users. Lastly, there is nicotine, showing that 428 respondents don’t use it, 847 are in the moderate categories, and 610 use it daily. This means that 22.7% of the people in the survey don’t use nicotine, and 32.4% use it daily. The summary that we got from the dataset highlights the varying levels of consumption for all three substances, showing a significant number of daily use among respondents for all three drugs. It also indicates that a notable portion of the population abstains from these substances altogether.

Project 3)

The null and alternative hypotheses of a \(\chi^2\) and a one way test are.

* \(H_0:\) the two categorical variables are independent, i.e., there is no relationship between them.

* \(H_A:\) the two categorical variables are dependent, i.e., there is a relationship between them.

2. From one of your stacked barplot of categorical variables, perform a chi-square test.

test_1 <- chisq.test(
  table(
    df_drugs$choc,
    df_drugs$nicotine
  )
)
Warning in stats::chisq.test(x, y, ...): Chi-squared approximation may be
incorrect
test_1

    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  table(df_drugs$choc, df_drugs$nicotine)
X-squared = 39.335, df = 36, p-value = 0.3229

Since the \(p\)-value \(p = 0.32 > 0.05\), we fail to reject \(H_0\) and conclude that choc and nicotine are independent.

1. From one of your boxplots of a categorical variable by group, perform an unpaired t-test, or an ANOVA if the categorical variable has more than two groups.

oneway.test(
  ascore ~ alcohol,
  data = df_drugs,
  var.equal = TRUE 
)

    One-way analysis of means

data:  ascore and alcohol
F = 2.9772, num df = 6, denom df = 1878, p-value = 0.006758

Since the \(p\)-value \(p = 0.007\) \(< 0.05\), we reject \(H_0\) and conclude that ascore and alcohol are dependent.
